newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-MATCH-FIX CASE MALAYSIAN SAYS CASH CAME FROM FRIEND.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MATCH-FIX CASE MALAYSIAN SAYS CASH CAME FROM FRIEND.

text.p: A Malaysian businessman accused in Britain's soccer match-fixing trial said on Wednesday a man who paid him thousands of pounds a month to forecast results was merely a kindly father figure.
"Win or lose, he will not moan or show any dissatisfaction -- he bets as a hobby," said Heng Suan Lim of his benefactor, a wealthy Indonesian businessman called Johannes Josef.
The prosecution accuses Lim, 31, of receiving around 500,000 pounds ($800,000) from various Asian sources which they allege he used to pay off members of a match-fixing ring in premier league soccer.
Lim, who stands accused with former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, former Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers and former Aston Villa striker John Fashanu, says he was paid only to forecast results.

"Mr Josef does not bet with any syndicate but with friends and associates on a friendly basis. It's very hurtful to suggest I am a representative of this betting syndicate," the otherwise phlegmatic Lim said in an impassioned plea to the jury.
Prosecutor Richard Calvert Smith detailed how the well-dressed Lim had embarked on a string of failed business ventures and indulged his passion for casinos since coming to Britain in 1988.
But his only apparent income came in regular contributions from Josef, whom Lim described as a close friend of his mother.
Lim says he also received money from his mother, an assistant manageress in a Kuala Lumpur nightclub.
Armed with copies of Lim's bank statements, Calvert-Smith pointed to large, specific sums of money paid into Lim's bank which were withdrawn in cash shortly afterwards.
At the same time, Lim was making regular phone calls to Josef, Fashanu, Grobbelaar and Segers, especially on the days of big soccer matches.
Lim has agreed he paid Grobbelaar and Segers for helping him with the match forecasts he provided for Josef, although he said the players would not offer predictions for their own team.
"If I asked 'how would your team do?' the answer would be 'of course, 100 percent we would win'. They were very loyal," said Lim.
"Surely the whole point of getting insiders was to get information," retorted Calvert-Smith. Lim did not reply but im said the players always insisted on being paid in cash. $ = 0.616 British Pounds)
